standard.title: Coping with changes and transitions
standard.description: plan, rehearse and reflect on strategies to cope with the different changes and transitions they experience, such as the changes associated with puberty
standard.prior_knowledge: Students have described personal qualities and explained how they contribute to developing identities (AC9HP2P01). They have some awareness of personal change but have not yet planned, rehearsed or reflected on coping strategies in a structured way, including for puberty.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students plan, rehearse and reflect on strategies to cope with the changes and transitions they experience, including those associated with puberty.

nodes.label: Changes and transitions — physical, social, emotional
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can discuss physical, social and emotional changes that occur as people get older and explore how these changes affect thinking and feeling.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least two types of changes (physical, social or emotional) that people experience as they grow older, and describe how one of these might affect how a person feels about themselves.
nodes.typical_width: Discuss physical, social and emotional changes across multiple transitions (e.g. primary to secondary school, puberty, family changes); explore how these changes interact and affect wellbeing.
wider: Explore the nature of family support networks in First Nations Australian communities and discuss how a wide range of family and community members support young people through changes and transitions.
Investigate how different cultures mark or celebrate the transition from childhood — examining what is valued and what support is provided.
nodes.hinge_reason: Identifying and understanding the types of changes is prerequisite to selecting and applying relevant coping strategies. Students who conflate physical changes with emotional ones, or cannot name the change type they are experiencing, will select poorly matched coping strategies.

response_modes.reason: Distinguishing physical, social and emotional changes requires a classification scaffold. A sorting activity (type of change → physical/social/emotional) followed by guided discussion of interactions between types builds the vocabulary and conceptual clarity needed for strategy planning.

success_criteria: Names at least two types of changes people experience as they grow older.
Classifies a given change as physical, social or emotional.
Describes how one type of change might affect a person's feelings or sense of self.

nodes.label: Sources of support for puberty and change
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify people or sources of information they can access when they have questions about puberty-related changes.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least two trusted people or reliable sources of information they could access for support or information about puberty.
nodes.typical_width: Identify a range of trusted people, organisations and information sources relevant to puberty and other changes; evaluate what makes a source trustworthy.
wider: Compare how young people in different contexts (urban/rural, cultural backgrounds, family structures) have access to different types of support, and discuss what this means for who young people turn to.
Design a simple 'where to go for help' resource for a younger student — identifying trusted people and reliable information sources with brief explanations of what each provides.

response_modes.reason: Students benefit from knowing a wide range of support options — trusted adults, peers, school resources, health professionals, reputable online resources — so they can identify accessible options for their specific situation. A single 'ask a parent' strategy is insufficient.

success_criteria: Names at least two people or sources of information they could turn to with questions about change or puberty.
Identifies at least one feature that makes a source of information trustworthy.
Distinguishes between a helpful and an unhelpful source of support or information.

nodes.label: Practising and reflecting on coping strategies
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can practise and refine coping strategies for dealing with challenges and changes, and evaluate the effectiveness of different responses.
nodes.minimum_width: Practise at least one coping strategy (e.g. positive self-talk, problem-solving, mindfulness, seeking help) and reflect on whether it was useful for a specific challenge or change.
nodes.typical_width: Practise a range of coping strategies across different challenge and change scenarios; compare strategies and reflect on which were most useful and why.
wider: Analyse a text or scenario where a character experiences and reacts to change — evaluate the effectiveness of the character's response and identify alternative strategies they could have used.
Develop a personal 'coping toolkit' that documents strategies that work for them across different types of challenges, with reflection on what each strategy is best suited for.

response_modes.reason: Strategy selection requires integrating understanding of the change type (node 1) with knowledge of available supports (node 2) and the specific strategy itself. The teaching focus should be on the match between situation type and strategy selection.

Different change and challenge contexts (school transitions, friendship changes, puberty, family change) benefit from different coping strategy emphases. Practising across contexts builds more flexible and transferable coping capability.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Coping strategy practice across diverse transition contexts (puberty, school change, family change, friendship change) is genuinely enriching — each context activates different strategies and builds more flexible coping capability.
success_criteria: Practises at least one coping strategy in a scenario or real context.
Describes whether the strategy was helpful and why.
Identifies a different strategy they could try if the first one did not work.
